title: Elevated intracranial pressure requiring decompressive craniectomy in a child with progressive primary angiitis of the central nervous system: a case report
case_prompt:
A previously healthy 5-year-old girl presented to the pediatric emergency department in generalized tonic-clonic status epilepticus and fever. Two months earlier, she had been treated for right medial clavicular sterile osteomyelitis with intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin. On arrival, she was febrile (39 °C), tachycardic (142 beats/min), tachypneic (36 breaths/min), and ill-appearing; blood pressure was 131/94 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% on a non-rebreather mask. After seizure termination with lorazepam and phenytoin, she exhibited hypoventilation requiring intubation. Neurologic examination showed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9, bilaterally reactive pupils, strong gag and cough reflexes, and no focal deficits. 

Initial investigations, including CSF studies (protein 0.28 g/L, glucose 4.1 mmol/L, 1 WBC/µL, 1 RBC/µL with rare lymphocytes), extensive infectious serologies (including tuberculosis and brucellosis), metabolic, hematologic, immunodeficiency, and genetic testing (primary immunodeficiency panel, whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing) were unrevealing. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 106 mg/L, ESR 47 mm/hr, von Willebrand factor >199.5%). Brain CT was normal; EEG showed diffuse nonspecific slowing without epileptiform discharges.

On hospital day 1, she developed signs of raised intracranial pressure—fixed dilated pupils, bradycardia, hypertension—and bilateral papilledema. CT angiography revealed multiple hypodensities, diffuse cerebral edema with a 5 mm midline shift, and impending right uncal herniation. First-tier intracranial pressure–lowering measures were instituted: head elevation to 30°, sedation, hyperventilation targeting PaCO₂ 35–40 mmHg, osmotherapy with 3% NaCl and mannitol, maintenance of MAP >60 mmHg, and normothermia. Concurrently, vasculitis–directed therapy was begun with IVIG (1 g/kg) and methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day for 5 days), followed by maintenance steroids and monthly cyclophosphamide. 

Brain MRI/MRA demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensity and swelling of the right cortex, vessel-wall enhancement of the middle cerebral arteries, and irregularity of the M1 and M2 segments bilaterally. Despite these therapies, she continued to show clinical and radiologic signs of refractory elevated intracranial pressure.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious encephalitis was considered given fever and seizures — “extensive infectious work-up including serological and cerebral spinal fluid tuberculosis and brucellosis … was unrevealing.”  
2. Metabolic, hematologic, immunodeficiency, and genetic disorders were excluded early in evaluation — “noninfectious causes including metabolic, hematological, immunodeficiency, and genetic diseases … was nonrevealing.”  
3. Systemic vasculitis was ruled out by negative serology and absence of systemic organ involvement — “There was no evidence of a systemic underlying condition known to cause CNS vasculitis, as indicated by negative serology and major vessel, renal, and liver venous and arterial ultrasound Doppler.”  
4. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis was excluded by lack of characteristic biopsy findings — “no hemophagocytic histiocytosis (HLH) features.”  
5. Malignancy was considered but brain biopsy showed gliosis without neoplastic features — “biopsies are crucial to exclude mimics such as malignancy … our patient’s lesional nonviable brain biopsy showed white-matter gliosis … but no nodules.”  
6. Angiography-negative cPACNS was less likely because imaging demonstrated medium‐vessel involvement — “angiography-negative (AN) disease … affects small cerebral vessels,” whereas “angiography-positive progressive (APP) disease … affects large/medium-sized vessels.”  
7. Primary angiitis of the CNS was supported by diffuse large-vessel inflammation on angiography and elevated inflammatory markers — “Primary blood vessel inflammation of the brain and/or spinal cord is the hallmark of cPACNS” and “In cPACNS, there is evidence of vascular inflammation, with elevated proinflammatory cytokines …”
final_diagnosis: childhood primary angiitis of the central nervous system
